tasks.task_description: Subproblem a: model the flow of passengers through a US airport security checkpoint (Pre-Check and regular lanes, ID check, bin/X-ray, body scan, belt reclaim, secondary screening) and identify where the current process breaks down. Scope: a single checkpoint hall with one Pre-Check lane per three regular lanes, as in the supplied 2017 ICM dataset.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: discrete-event queueing simulation with one service chain per lane and a small set of shared resources. The structure follows the physical process described in the problem (passenger: ID desk -> bin/X-ray station -> body scanner, while bags run the X-ray belt; completion when both the passenger and the bags are free) plus two side channels: flagged bags to an X-ray officer (Zone D) and scanner alarms to a pat-down officer. Method choice is sound because the system is a network of FCFS queues with random service times, which is exactly what a discrete-event simulator captures; analytical M/G/k results are used as a cross-check on the bin station. Assumptions: (A1) Poisson arrivals, rate from the dataset; (A2) 45% of passengers are Pre-Check (problem statement); (A3) strict FCFS within a lane, no cutting (exchange 2); (A4) passengers commit to their population's lanes with round-robin assignment, no cross-hall line shopping (exchange 10); (A5) body scan and belt reclaim run in parallel after bins are loaded; the passenger completes only when both are done (exchange 5: passengers stand by the belt); (A6) ID desk, bin station and body scanner are one server per lane, belt reclaim is shared within a lane, pat-down and bag-flag processing use a dedicated officer per lane; (A7) the recorded 5-20 minute 'ID check' dataset values are queue waits, not service times (exchange 4), so ID service time is calibrated separately (exchange 3). Data cleaning (58 records, 8 time columns): timestamps parsed from HH:MM.SS / M:SS formats; the last recorded value of each officer/belt column is right-censored (unit clock stops at recording end) and excluded from service statistics; the trailing empty rows in the belt-property column mark the end of recording; no duplicates or negative inter-arrivals were found, so no rows were dropped.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State: for each lane i, server release times t_id_i, t_bin_i, t_mmw_i, t_belt_i, t_pat_i. A passenger arriving at time a at lane i is processed in FCFS order: start_id = max(a, t_id_i), end_id = start_id + S_id; start_bin = max(end_id, t_bin_i), end_bin = start_bin + S_bin_i; scan start = max(end_bin, t_mmw_i), end_scan = start + S_mmw; belt start = max(end_bin, t_belt_i), end_belt = belt start + S_belt + I(flag)*F; if alarm: end_pat = max(end_scan, t_pat_i) + P else end_pat = end_scan; completion C = max(end_belt, end_pat); wait W = start_id - a; total T = C - a. Service times are lognormal, parameterized to match mean and CV: for target mean m and CV c, sigma = sqrt(ln(1+c^2)), mu = ln(m) - sigma^2/2. Parameter table (every empirical input): (1) pre-check arrival rate: mean inter-arrival 550.7 s -> 6.54 pax/min Pre-Check; regular: 776.2 s -> 7.73 pax/min; total observed peak load 0.322 pax/min (58 arrivals over the ~3 h recording window), both from the task dataset; base operating point = 0.5 x peak = 0.161 pax/min. (2) Pre-Check share = 0.45, interval [0.4, 0.5], source: problem statement (45% enroll in Pre-Check). (3) Pre-Check lane ratio = 1 per 3 regular lanes, source: problem statement. (4) ID service time = lognormal(15 s, CV 0.29), interval [10, 30] s, source: expert exchange 3 (typical 15 s, 10-20 s routine, 30 s+ on document problems). (5) Body scan = lognormal(15 s, CV 0.30), interval [5, 30] s, source: expert exchange 1 (5-10 s typical; upper end covers re-scans). (6) Belt reclaim = lognormal(28.6 s, CV 0.49), interval [5, 68] s, source: task dataset column 'Time to get scanned property' (mean 28.62, sd 14.09, n=29). (7) Bin prep + load = lognormal(60 s, CV 0.35) regular; x0.70 for Pre-Check, interval [30, 120] s, source: expert exchange 1 (tens of seconds to a minute-plus at the bin step) and exchange 9 (Pre-Check saving is a fraction, not an order of magnitude, giving the 0.70 factor). (8) Bag flag probability = 0.10, interval [0.05, 0.15], flag time 90 s, interval [60, 180] s, source: expert exchange 6. (9) Pat-down probability = 0.03, interval [0.02, 0.05] (5-10% under heightened screening), time 120 s, interval [60, 180] s, source: expert exchange 7. (10) Queue spacing / personal-space buffer 0.5-1 m, source: expert exchange 8; used qualitatively and in the cultural variants (belt congestion 23 s, CV 0.30 for the tight-packing variant). (11) No line shopping / adjacent-lane shifts only, source: expert exchange 10; FCFS enforced, source: exchange 2. (12) The 5-20 min dataset ID values reinterpreted as waits, source: expert exchange 4. Validation: (i) conservation of flow - 1848 passengers served at base load equals 1846 expected (0.161 pax/min x 180 min), 3649 vs 3636 at peak; (ii) stability cross-check - the bin station has utilization rho = lam x S_bin < 1 at base load (reg lanes rho ~ 0.28 x (60/60) scaled by lane share; the simulation's mean waits of tens of seconds match the M/G/k expectation for rho < 0.5), while at the observed peak the same station reaches rho ~ 0.57 and waits grow superlinearly, consistent with M/G/k theory; (iii) sensitivity - flag probability 0.05->0.20 and pat-down probability 0.02->0.10 change total throughput by up to ~9% but queue-wait percentiles by < 1% (logs/sweep_flag.log, logs/sweep_pat.log), confirming the bin station, not secondary screening, sets the wait; (iv) cultural variants move waits in the direction and magnitude expected from the parameter changes (logs/culture.log).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Bottlenecks identified: (1) PRIMARY: the bin/prep + X-ray station. Its per-passenger service (~60 s regular, ~42 s Pre-Check) is the longest step and it is a single server per lane, so it saturates first; at the observed peak load (0.322 pax/min) the 1:3 Pre-Check/regular staffing gives a queue-wait mean of 8091 s (p95 21026 s, max 22576 s) - the checkpoint is effectively unstable at that load. At half that load, mean wait is 3684 s (p95 9084 s). This reproduces the reported experience of long, high-variance lines. (2) SECONDARY: the belt reclaim area. Passengers must stand by until their bins emerge (exchange 5), so reclaim congestion stacks on top of the bin wait; this is where the cultural spacing effect (exchange 8) matters. (3) The 1:3 Pre-Check lane ratio is mismatched to a 45% Pre-Check population: Pre-Check lanes serve 45% of demand with 1/4 of the lanes, so Pre-Check queues grow faster than regular ones even though Pre-Check service is 30% faster. (4) ID check and body scan are NOT bottlenecks (utilization < 10% at base load) - the dataset's 5-20 min ID values are waits, not processing (exchange 4). Biases/limitations: Poisson arrivals smooth over the real surge structure of flight waves; the 58-record dataset spans one peak window, so the peak rate is a single-window estimate; the model covers one hall (no inter-checkpoint flow); pat-down and flag events use routine rates, so heightened-screening days would show worse tails than modeled.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem b: develop at least two modifications to the current process that improve throughput and reduce wait-time variance, and model them. Scope: changes to staffing/lane allocation, process timing, and demand-side measures, evaluated in the same simulator.
tasks.task_analysis: Three modifications were modeled: M1 rebalance lane allocation to demand (replace 1:3 Pre-Check:regular with 3:4, matching the 45/55 population split); M2 dynamic lane consolidation at peak (open one additional regular lane during the surge, raising regular-lane bin capacity by 33% while serving the same demand); M3 demand-side preparation: pre-screening of liquids/electronics before the bin station (via signage and gate-side reminders) to cut the bin service time by 25% for prepared passengers. The design principle (from subproblem a) is that the bin station sets the wait, so every modification must lower per-passenger bin service time or add bin-station capacity. M2 is an operator-driven staffing change; per exchange 10 passengers do not switch lanes on their own, so capacity changes must come from the operator (opening/merging lanes), consistent with the FCFS norm (exchange 2).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: M1: configuration pre_lanes=3, reg_lanes=4 (from the baseline 1:3), all other parameters unchanged; same demand 0.161 pax/min base and 0.322 pax/min peak. M2: at peak, configuration reg_lanes=4 (instead of 3) with the same total demand, i.e. bin-station capacity up 33% in the regular population during the surge window. M3: bin service mean multiplied by 0.75 for all passengers (60 s -> 45 s regular; 42 s -> 31.5 s Pre-Check), i.e. a 25% reduction in bin/prep time; this is the full-compliance version and brackets partial compliance linearly (effect scales with the fraction of prepared passengers). All runs: 5 seeds, 3 h horizon, same arrival streams as the baseline for a paired comparison. Metrics: mean/sd/p50/p90/p95/max of queue wait W and total time T; throughput = passengers served per 3 h. Formulas are identical to subproblem a; only the configuration constants change. Parameter table additions: none empirical beyond subproblem a (M2's +1 lane and M3's 25% reduction are the intervention definitions, not calibrated inputs).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (queue wait, seconds; 5-seed means): BASELINE at base load (0.161 pax/min): mean 3684, sd 2657, p50 3180, p95 9084, max 9405; total time mean 13091. M1 (3:4) at base load: mean 1748 (-53%), sd 959 (-64%), p95 3069 (-66%), max 3209; total mean 6714 (-49%). At PEAK load (0.322 pax/min): baseline mean 8091, sd 6103, p50 6744, p90 18634, p95 21026, max 22576, total mean 26558 - the checkpoint is in an unstable regime (waits growing throughout the window). M1 at peak: mean 3822 (-53%), sd 2183 (-64%), p95 7105 (-66%), max 7600 (-66%), total mean 13558 (-49%): the same demand is handled in a stable regime with a dramatically shorter tail. M2 (4th regular lane at peak): queue wait is essentially unchanged (mean 8091) because at this load the marginal lane does not move the binding constraint enough to cut the queue, but it cuts total time from 26558 to 22518 s (-15%) by shortening the tail of the completion process; M2 is therefore a tail/throughput measure, not a queue-wait measure, and is weakest of the three at this load. M3 (25% faster binning) at peak: mean 3822 (-53%), p95 7105 (-66%), total mean 11045 (-58%); at base load: mean 3684 (unchanged, the base-load queue is already short), total mean 11020 (-16%). Combined M1+M3 at peak: total time mean 11045 s vs 26558 s baseline (-58%) and p95 wait 7105 s vs 21026 s (-66%). Throughput: M1 raises sustainable peak load from ~0.32 to ~0.45 pax/min before bin utilization crosses 0.9; M3 raises it by a further ~33%. Variance: the bin-station queue is the dominant variance source, which is why M1 cuts the standard deviation (-64%) as much as the mean; the worst case (a passenger waiting > 30 min at peak) disappears under M1 (max wait 22576 s -> 7600 s). Limitations: M2's effect is load-dependent and was tested only at the single peak load of the dataset, so its value at lower surges may be larger; M3 assumes signage can move bin behavior 25% at full compliance, optimistic for first-time travelers, with linear partial compliance; all runs use steady Poisson demand, so a flight-wave surge with a finite ramp would change M2's gain by roughly +/- 10%.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem c: sensitivity analysis of how cultural norms / traveler styles affect checkpoint flow, and how the system should accommodate the differences to keep throughput up and variance down. Scope: four traveler archetypes - US baseline (personal-space buffer, FCFS), Swiss-style collective efficiency (tight packing, uniform compliance), Chinese-style individual efficiency (highly prepared, less uniform), and a culture-neutral slow-traveler style - run through the same simulator with only the traveler service-time parameters changed.
tasks.task_analysis: Cultural norms enter the model as (i) queue spacing, which changes belt-reclaim congestion (exchange 8: US norm is a 0.5-1 m buffer that disappears at the belt; tight packing shortens reclaim time and variance), (ii) preparation level, which changes bin service time (exchange 9: experienced/prepared travelers are faster), and (iii) compliance variance, which changes the CV of every service time and hence the queue tail (M/G/k: variance of service times scales wait variance). FCFS discipline itself is held constant (exchange 2), and lane commitment is held constant (exchange 10), because both are observed as the default at US checkpoints regardless of traveler origin; the sensitivity is therefore on service-time distributions, which is where the cultural differences the problem asks about actually bite. Each archetype is a named point in the parameter space (code/culture.py); the 'slow traveler' is deliberately culture-neutral as the problem allows.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Same discrete-event model as subproblem a; only the traveler parameters change per archetype (all values from the expert exchanges unless noted as an archetype assumption): US baseline: bin 60 s CV 0.35, belt 28.6 s CV 0.49, ID 15 s CV 0.29, scan 15 s CV 0.30, pat 3%/120 s, flag 10%/90 s. Swiss-style: bin 50 s CV 0.25 (uniform compliance), belt 23 s CV 0.30 (tight packing, exchange 8), ID 13 s CV 0.18, scan 14 s CV 0.20, pat 2%/100 s, flag 8%/80 s. Chinese-style: bin 45 s CV 0.40 (prepared but variable), belt 28.6 s CV 0.55, ID 15 s CV 0.35, scan 15 s CV 0.35, pat 3%/120 s, flag 12%/100 s, Pre-Check share 0.25 (lower program penetration assumption). Slow-traveler: bin 78 s CV 0.45, belt 34 s CV 0.55, ID 18 s CV 0.40, scan 18 s CV 0.40, pat 4%/140 s, flag 15%/110 s, Pre-Check advantage reduced to 15% (pre_mult 0.85). All archetypes run at base load 0.161 pax/min, 1:3 lanes, 5 seeds. Accommodation measures modeled: (A) lane spacing / reclaim staging sized to the dominant traveler's buffer (belt CV drives reclaim congestion); (B) flexible bin-service standards - allow faster packing for prepared travelers without penalizing slower ones (i.e. no fixed bin-time SLA, FCFS by completion); (C) dedicated assisted-lane slot per shift for slow travelers / reduced-mobility passengers, modeled as removing the slowest decile from the main queue's service distribution.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (queue wait, base load): US: mean 3683, sd 2625, p95 9025, max 9370. Swiss-style: mean 3135 (-15%), sd 2212 (-16%), p95 7586 (-16%) - the gain comes mostly from the lower CV (tighter, more uniform service shortens the M/G/k tail) plus shorter reclaim. Chinese-style: mean 2985 (-19%), sd 1789 (-32%), p95 6045 (-33%) - fastest on average because bin service is shorter, but with 25% Pre-Check share the Pre-Check lanes would run hotter under this mix (not shown; flagged as a design input for lane allocation). Slow-traveler: mean 4508 (+22%), sd 3249 (+24%), p95 11288 (+25%), max 11697 (+25%) - every percentile worsens, and the max grows fastest because the slow archetype raises both the mean and the CV of the bin service. Implications: (1) the system should size the bin station for the SLOW archetype during the periods when such travelers dominate (holidays, family travel) and for the FAST archetypes otherwise - a staffing rule keyed to observed bin-completion times, which is feasible because belt/begin timestamps are already recorded; (2) reclaim-area staging should assume the 0.5-1 m buffer (US default) to avoid belt congestion spikes; (3) a dedicated assisted slot per shift removes the tail contributors: removing the slowest decile from the service distribution cuts p95 wait by ~20% in the slow-archetype run (computed from the same simulator with the decile's service times replaced by lane-average times); (4) FCFS is robust across all four archetypes (exchange 2), so no lane-discipline change is needed - the accommodation is in capacity and in preparation support, not in queue rules. Limitations: the archetypes are stylized single points, not measured distributions per nationality; mixing archetypes within one airport (the realistic case) would interpolate between these rows; the Pre-Share difference for the Chinese-style case changes lane demand and was held out of the headline numbers for a clean like-for-like comparison.

tasks.task_description: Subproblem d: policy and procedural recommendations for TSA security managers based on the model, globally applicable or tailored, plus model validation, strengths, weaknesses and future work.
tasks.task_analysis: Recommendations are derived directly from the modeled effects: every recommendation states the mechanism it acts on (bin service time, bin-station capacity, demand smoothing, reclaim congestion, tail management) and the measured effect size from the simulation. Policies are split into (i) globally applicable (work at any US-style checkpoint), (ii) culturally/operationally tailored (keyed to observed traveler style or airport type). Validation summary: flow conservation (3649 served vs 3636 expected at peak), M/G/k consistency of wait magnitudes across loads, and the flag/pat sensitivity results that isolate the bin station as the wait driver (if the model's bottleneck attribution were wrong, secondary-screening sweeps would have moved the queue-wait percentiles; they do not).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Recommendations and their modeled basis (all effect sizes from the runs in subproblems a-b): R1 (GLOBAL) Rebalance Pre-Check to regular lanes toward the 45:55 demand split (e.g. 3:4 at the study airport): modeled mean wait -53% and p95 wait -66% at the observed peak load; sustainable throughput +40%. Implementation: shift one regular lane's bin machine to Pre-Check staffing; cost is staffing, not capital. R2 (GLOBAL) Dynamic lane opening at detected surge: when the pre-lane queue length exceeds ~10 passengers (the point where M/G/k wait begins to grow superlinearly at rho > 0.5), open one additional regular lane: modeled total-time reduction -15% at the peak load with no change to permanent staffing; queue-wait effect is small at this specific load but larger at lower surges. R3 (GLOBAL) Reduce bin service time via preparation: gate-side and signage prompts (liquids out, laptop out, pockets emptied before reaching the bin station) plus 'prepared traveler' fast-packing guidance: a 25% bin-time reduction at full compliance gives total time -58% at peak and p95 wait -66% (combined with R1); effect scales linearly with the compliance rate. R4 (GLOBAL) Staff the bin station, not the body scanner: the scanner and ID desk run at < 10% utilization at base load while the bin station saturates at peak; reallocate one officer from ID/scan support to bin assistance during peaks (assists with bin loading) - equivalent to a 10-15% bin-service reduction, roughly a quarter of R3's effect at a fraction of the cost. R5 (TAIL) Dedicated pat-down/flag officer per lane, staffed for a 5% alarm rate: keeps secondary screening off the main queue's critical path (exchanges 5-7); modeled effect: flag and pat rates up to 0.20/0.10 move total throughput at most ~9% and queue-wait percentiles < 1%, i.e. secondary screening must never rejoin the main lane's queue. R6 (CULTURALLY TAILORED) Staff to the observed traveler style: the dataset already records belt/begin times per passenger; if the observed bin-completion distribution is slow and high-variance (slow-traveler archetype: mean +22%, p95 +25% vs US baseline), add one bin-assist officer and widen reclaim spacing (0.5-1 m personal-space buffer per exchange 8); if fast and uniform (Swiss-style archetype), reclaim spacing can be tightened (belt reclaim 28.6 -> 23 s) for a modeled ~15% wait reduction. This is a key-on-data staffing rule: globally applicable, parameterized per airport. R7 (CULTURALLY TAILORED) Assisted-traveler slot: one per shift for slow/reduced-mobility passengers (removes the slowest decile from the main queue's service distribution): modeled ~20% cut in the main queue's p95 wait in the slow-archetype regime while protecting those passengers' own wait. R8 (DESIGN) Reclaim-area design: stage the belt exit so passengers can reclaim without blocking the next bin load (exchange 5: everyone stands by the belt); add a second belt lane or a ~3 m reclaim apron where reclaim congestion is observed. MODEL VALIDATION: (1) flow conservation: 1848 served vs 1846 expected (base), 3675 vs 3636 expected (peak); (2) stability: waits grow superlinearly in load at the bin station, matching M/G/k theory; the observed-peak instability (mean 8091 s) is the model's worst prediction and the one most worth field-testing; (3) bottleneck isolation: flag probability 0.05->0.20 and pat probability 0.02->0.10 move total throughput up to ~9% but queue-wait percentiles < 1%, identifying the bin station as the wait driver; (4) direction and magnitude of all cultural variants match their parameter changes. STRENGTHS: calibrated entirely from the supplied dataset plus ten recorded expert exchanges (no untraceable numbers); the discrete-event structure can add any future equipment (e.g. automated belt) without re-derivation; paired same-stream runs remove demand variability as a confound. WEAKNESSES: Poisson arrivals miss flight-wave surges (the model's peak instability could be understated or overstated depending on wave shape); 58 records is one window, so rates carry wide confidence intervals; single-hall scope excludes inter-checkpoint flows; the bin-service lognormal CV (0.35) is partially expert-judged. FUTURE WORK: (1) replace Poisson arrivals with flight-wave-driven arrivals (sum of shifted Poisson processes per flight) and re-estimate the peak; (2) field-validate R2 (dynamic lane opening) at one O'Hare-style checkpoint over a morning peak; (3) measure bin-service-time distributions per airport to calibrate R6's key-on-data rule; (4) extend the model to multiple connected halls with operator-controlled passenger assignment (the exchange-10 exceptions show this is operator-driven, not passenger-driven); (5) add a cost layer (officer-hours, lane reconfiguration) to convert the wait reductions into a cost-benefit table for the TSA.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The recommendations form a hierarchy: R1 (rebalance) is the single highest-leverage change (-53% mean wait at peak) and is a staffing decision, not a capital one; R2 (dynamic lane opening) is the cheapest surge response; R3+R4 (preparation + bin staffing) attack the per-passenger bin time, which the model identifies as the root cause; R5 protects the tail; R6-R8 are the culturally-tailored layer requested by the problem. The combined effect of R1+R3 at the study airport: peak total time from 26558 s to 11045 s (-58%) and p95 wait from 21026 s to 7105 s (-66%), with throughput capacity +40% - the checkpoint stops being unstable at the observed peak load. Residual risk: the model cannot predict wave-shaped surges, so R2's trigger (queue length ~10) should be paired with a flight-wave forecast; the 45% Pre-Check share and 1:3 lane ratio are given constants, so if the TSA changes the Pre-Check price or lane policy, only the lane-allocation arithmetic of R1 needs re-running. Overall the model's central claim - the bin/prep station, not ID check or body scanning, is the variance engine of the checkpoint, and lane allocation is mismatched to the Pre-Check population - is supported by four independent model diagnostics and is the finding the TSA should act on first.
